title: Oven-baked chicken tenders
skill: Trimming raw chicken into strips and checking 165°F

notes.text: For more than 4, use two sheet pans, one on each of the two middle racks, and swap them halfway through baking.

move.title: One station, start to finish
move.body: This is the unit's mastery week: you set up the raw-meat station yourself, the way you practised in the drill, and cook from it without help. You'll trim chicken breasts into even strips, bread them with one dry hand and one wet hand, and bake them crisp on a hot sheet pan until the thickest strip reads 165°F. A honey-mustard dip goes alongside.

why.title: Even strips, one finish
why.body: A chicken breast is thick at one end and thin at the other. Cut straight across, the thin pieces dry out while the thick ones are still under 165°F. Cutting the thick end into narrower strips makes every piece about the same thickness, so the whole pan is done together.

why.title: The white tendon
why.body: The tender, the loose strip on the underside of each breast, has a tough white tendon at its thick end. It turns rubbery when cooked. Trim it off with the tip of the knife, along with any thick fat.

why.title: Toast the crumbs first
why.body: Fried chicken is golden because hot oil browns the crumbs. In the oven there's much less oil, so the crumbs would stay pale. Toasting the panko in a little oil before breading gives it the color and crunch up front.

why.title: One dry hand, one wet hand
why.body: Use one hand only for the flour and crumbs and the other only for the egg. If both hands go in everything, your fingers end up coated in thick paste. Keeping them apart keeps the breading even, and only one hand touches raw chicken in the egg.

why.title: A hot pan crisps the bottom
why.body: Strips laid on a cold pan steam on the bottom and go soggy. Heating the oiled sheet pan in the oven first means the bottoms start to crisp the moment the chicken touches it.

wrong.sign: The breading falls off in patches
wrong.fix: The chicken was wet, or the flour step was skipped. Press crumbs into bare spots before baking. Next time, pat the strips dry and flour every side.
The crumbs weren't toasted long enough. Bake 2 more minutes, checking they don't go past golden.

wrong.sign: The thinnest strips read 175°F and the thickest 160°F
wrong.fix: The strips weren't even. Take the done ones off and give the thick ones 2 more minutes. Next time, cut the thick end narrower.
Stir in a little more honey, a teaspoon at a time.

quiz.q: Why cut the thick end of a breast into narrower strips?
choices: So every strip is the same thickness and finishes together
quiz.explain: Even pieces reach 165°F at the same time.

quiz.q: Why use one dry hand and one wet hand?
choices: So your fingers don't clump with breading
So you can work faster with both
quiz.explain: One hand for flour and crumbs, the other for the egg.

quiz.q: Why toast the panko before breading?
choices: The oven alone won't brown it the way frying does
quiz.explain: Toasted crumbs come out of the oven golden.

quiz.q: What temperature do the tenders need?

substitutions.note: Chop the oats fine and toast them the same way.
Cornstarch coats the strips the same way, and the egg sticks to it.

steps.text: Set up your station as in this week's drill: a clean counter, the raw-meat board on a damp paper towel, a plate for the raw chicken, a clean plate for the cooked, a dishpan or sink of hot, soapy water, and the thermometer calibrated and within reach.
steps.tip: This is the mastery check. Cook from here on your own; the adult watches but doesn't step in.

steps.text: Put a rack in the middle of the oven. Spread the pan's oil over the sheet pan, set it on the rack, and heat the oven to 425°F.
Stir the panko and the breading's oil in the skillet over medium heat until golden. Tip it into the medium bowl to cool.
steps.look: Light golden brown all through, not just in spots.

steps.text: In the small bowl, stir together the mayonnaise, mustard, and honey. Taste it and refrigerate it.
Turn off the stove. Mix the flour, paprika, garlic powder, and pepper on a plate. Line up the flour, then the shallow dish for the eggs, then the bowl of panko, with the raw-chicken plate at the end.
Crack the eggs into a shallow dish, add the water, and beat them with the fork until smooth.
Wash your hands with soap and throw the shells away.

Lay each breast on the raw-meat board. Pull off the loose tender underneath and trim its white tendon. Trim any thick fat from the breast. Cut the breast lengthwise into strips about ¾ inch thick, cutting the thick end narrower so every strip is close to the same thickness. Pat them dry and sprinkle them with the chicken's salt.
steps.look: About 12 strips, all close to ¾ inch thick.

steps.text: Throw the paper towels away. Wash your hands, the knife, and the board in the hot, soapy water.

Pick one hand for dry and one for wet. With your dry hand, drop a strip in the flour and turn it to coat. Lift it into the egg, and with your wet hand, turn it and let the extra drip off. Drop it in the panko and coat it with your dry hand, pressing the crumbs on. Set it on the raw-chicken plate and bread the rest the same way.
Wash your hands with soap. Throw away what's left of the flour, egg, and crumbs, which have touched raw chicken, and put the dishes in the hot, soapy water.
Take the hot sheet pan out with oven mitts and lay the strips on it with your fingers, 1 inch apart. Return it to the oven.
Wash your hands and put the raw-chicken plate in the hot, soapy water.
Bake, turning the strips once halfway with the spatula.
steps.look: Golden on both sides and sizzling.

steps.text: Take the pan out and check the two thickest strips from the side: each needs at least 165°F. If one doesn't, bake 2 more minutes and check again.
Move the tenders to the clean plate with the spatula and serve them with the dip. Wash the thermometer probe in hot, soapy water.
